content.thinking:
I need to write this postmortem using placeholders rather than actual figures, tracing the chain from symptom to cause: account pages slowed down with p50 latency rising noticeably while error rates stayed roughly flat, which suggests the issue was a performance bottleneck rather than outright failures. I should cite the relevant data points for latency before, during, and at peak severity, alongside error counts for comparison.

Tracing further, every request was missing the summary cache and falling back to rebuilding from purchase history, which I'd back with the cache-miss and fallback evidence. The deeper cause is a deployment that changed the cache port, causing connection refusals -- I can rule out a bad code deploy since the diff only touched configuration, and I can rule out a feature flag change since the provider showed no recent flag activity in that window; the timing also lines up since the port change preceded the onset while an earlier unrelated change happened too long before to be the cause, and the rollback confirms it.

For why the fallback itself was so slow, I only have one unverified source pointing to quadratic behavior in the purchase-history read path, so I need to flag that as unverified rather than confirmed, while the cache-port failure itself is well-supported by logs and counts as a verified root cause.

Now I'm working out the contributing factors -- no pre-deploy check for cache port reachability, no load testing of the fallback path, alerting delays, and the auto-sync being off as a downstream effect of the rollback -- and mapping each to a new action item: validating cache ports before deploy, adding alerts on cache hit ratio drops, assigning an owner to confirm correct production config values, and performance-testing the fallback path under realistic data volumes. I'm being careful to avoid including specific numbers in my action item descriptions.

For the impact section, I'm noting pages were slower but not failing outright, errors stayed within normal range, and there were some client disconnects that might reflect shopper impatience, though I'll avoid speculating on that. For detection, I'm noting when the alert fired, how long the paging rule took, and when the rollback actually occurred, keeping the timestamps minimal. For assumptions, I'm flagging that the fallback cost estimate wasn't actually tested and that cache health is still a candidate explanation since the real port configuration was never verified.

action_items.item: Have the cache's owner confirm which port the summary cache really listens on and correct the cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml, which still says the refused port.
Add a pre-deploy or post-rollout check that the configured cache host and port accept connections, and block or flag the rollout when they do not.
Add a load test of the cache-miss fallback path using a very long purchase history, with a latency budget, so that any cache outage is known to be a small slowdown.
Alert on summary cache connection errors and a falling cache hit ratio, so a cache outage is noticed without waiting for the latency rule.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages. The alert series (median latency) rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and peaked at {series_at_worst}. Failed requests did not rise beyond normal variation: the error rate was {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before, peaking at {errors_at_worst}.
Every account-page request failed its summary cache lookup with 'connection refused' and fell back to computing the summary from the purchase history. Pages stayed correct but were slow.

The cache lookups were refused because deploy 0d8e826 changed the cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.3} to {D1.4}, and the cache refuses connections on the new port. Ruled out: bad application code, because the diff touched only configuration (D1); a flag change, because the flag provider showed no recent changes (T15); the earlier deploy P1, which went out hours before the onset, whereas P2 landed one minute before it. Rolling back the deploy brought latency back to normal, which confirms the trigger.

The fallback is far more expensive than the cache hit it replaces. A static reading of the source (unverified, since nothing ran it) says the lifetime-spend calculation rebuilds its running total from scratch for each purchase. That makes it quadratic in the length of the purchase history, a cost that stayed hidden while the cache answered. The evidence does not show measured purchase-history sizes or a profile of the fallback.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that the cache address in a config change is reachable before or after rollout. A port change that the cache refuses reached production.

The fallback path's cost with large purchase histories was not seen to be tested, so a cache outage, which the design treats as survivable, became a large slowdown. The proposed fix is still unmerged.

Nothing was seen alerting on cache connection failures or a collapsing cache hit ratio. Only the latency alert fired, and its paging rule waits {rule_waits} before firing, so the page came after the onset.
After the rollback, automatic sync of io-shop remains off, so nothing merged, including the fix, reaches production until it is turned back on.

input.executive_summary: For a little over five minutes ({duration}), account pages on the shop were noticeably slower. Typical latency went from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at worst. Pages kept loading and the error rate stayed within its normal range ({errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before), so the harm was slowness, not failures. A configuration change had pointed the shop at the wrong port for its summary cache. Pages then had to recompute their summaries on every visit, and that recomputation is expensive. Argus rolled the change back and latency returned to normal. A fix that makes the recomputation cheap has been proposed as a draft pull request and is awaiting review. The configured cache port still needs to be corrected by the cache's owner.

got_lucky: The slowdown did not turn into failed requests: the error rate stayed within its normal range, so shoppers saw slow pages rather than errors.
The config change was the only recent change in the window, which made the rollback target clear.
went_well: Argus tied the onset to the deploy that landed just before it and read the diff. Its rollback restored normal latency, and the mitigation was confirmed.
The deploy diff was read and the flag provider history checked, which let the investigation rule out a code change and a flag change.
Code-Fix proposed a draft fix and flagged the config port that still needs correcting.
went_wrong: A one-line port change reached production without any check that the cache was reachable.
The cache is optional by design, yet losing it made pages much slower because the fallback path was expensive.
Automatic sync of io-shop is still off after the incident, so nothing merged reaches it.

input.root_cause: The production config change pointed the optional summary cache at a port where it refuses connections, so every account-page request took the fallback path. That path is, by an unverified static reading of the code, quadratic in the length of the purchase history, so losing the cache made every page much slower. The cache outage alone does not explain a slowdown this large.
input.symptom: Account pages were slow to load
